title: Systemic HDAC Inhibition Changes Glutamatergic Neuronal Properties in Prefrontal Cortex and Ventrobasal Thalamus
content: Reversible protein acetylation controlled by histone deacetylases (HDACs) regulates neuronal gene expression and, increasingly, membrane physiology. We previously showed that pedunculopontine nucleus (PPN) gamma-band oscillations require class IIa HDAC activity, whereas class I inhibition was comparatively benign for that readout. Whether systemic HDAC inhibition acts uniformly across the forebrain, and across different neuronal nuclei, is unknown. Here we administered acute single systemic doses of the class I inhibitor MS275 (entinostat) and the class IIa inhibitor MC1568 to mice and performed whole-cell recordings in two functionally distinct, anatomically unconnected structures: medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) and the ventrobasal complex (VB) of the thalamus. In mPFC pyramidal neurons we assessed short-term plasticity using paired-pulse stimulation and quantifying paired-pulse ratio (PPR); in VB neurons we quantified action-potential amplitude and the maximal rate of rise of the spike from phase-plot analysis. MS275 shifted PPR from facilitation toward depression on both mPFC and VB glutamatergic transmission, a significant change relative to vehicle, while MC1568 produced an intermediate, non-significant effect. In addition, MS275      reduced action-potential amplitude and markedly decreased the maximal rate of rise (dV/dt) of the spike in VB neurons. Thus, class I HDAC inhibition predominantly affected presynaptic glutamate release whilst affecting intrinsic properties of thalamocortical neurons. These results suggest that the consequences of systemic HDAC inhibition are class- and region-specific.
